Etymology

The name Old Goa was first used in the 1960s in the address of the Konkani monthly magazine, dedicated to spread the devotion of the Sacred Heart, Dor Mhoineachi Rotti, which was shifted to the Basilica of Bom Jesus in 1964. Postal letters were returned to the sender, as the name "Old Goa" was unknown then, according to then- and long-time editor of the monthly, the great Goan historian late Padre Moreno de Souza, SJ.

The village panchayat uses the name Sé-Old Goa, while the post office and the Archaeological Survey of India use the name Velha Goa.

The place is known as Saibachem Goem (referring to St. Francis Xavier as saib, i.e., master), Pornnem Goem, Adlem Goem or just Goem in Konkani.

Velha Goa should not be confused with another former Goan capital, Goa Velha, lying some villages away in the south. The names Vhoddlem Goem and Thorlem Goem refer to Goa Velha, while Goem, besides referring to Velha Goa—i.e., Old Goa—also refers to the whole state of Goa in some contexts (Old Goa).

History
The city was founded in the 15th century as a port on the banks of the Mandovi river by the rulers of the Bijapur Sultanate. It was built to replace Govapuri, which lay a few kilometres to the south and had been used as a port by the Kadamba and Vijayanagar kings. Old Goa was the second capital after Bijapur of the rule of Adil Shahi Dynasty. It was surrounded by a moat and contained the shah's palace, mosques, and temples. The city was captured by the Portuguese and was under Portuguese rule from 1510 as the administrative seat of Portuguese India.

The viceroy's residence was transferred in 1759 to the future capital, Panjim (a village about 9 kilometres to its west). Few remnants, if any, of the pre-Portuguese period remain at Old Goa.

During the mid-16th century, the Portuguese colony of Goa, especially Velha Goa, was the center of Christianisation in the East. The city was evangelized by all religious orders, since all of them had their headquarters there. The population was roughly 200,000 by 1543. Malaria and cholera epidemics ravaged the city in the 17th century and it was largely abandoned, only having a remaining population of 1,500 in 1775. It was then that the viceroy moved to Panjim. It continued to be the de jure capital of Goa until 1843, when the capital was shifted to Panjim (Ponnjê in Konkani, Nova Goa in Portuguese and Panaji in Hindi). The abandoned city came to be known as "Velha Goa" (in Portuguese, 'Old Goa'), to distinguish it from the new capital Nova Goa (Panjim) and probably also Goa Velha (also meaning "Old Goa"), which was the Portuguese name for the town on the old site of Govapuri.

Velha Goa was incorporated into the Republic of India after its annexation in 1961, with the rest of Goa. It retains its religious significance in modern-day Goa, notably in its relations with Roman Catholicism. The Archbishop of Goa and Daman holds title as the Patriarch of the East Indies. Old Goa contains churches including the Se Cathedral (the seat of the Archbishop of Goa), the Church and Convent of St. Francis of Assisi, the Chapel of Our Lady of the Mount, the Church of St. Caetano and, notably, the Basilica of Bom Jesus which contains the relics of Saint Francis Xavier, who is celebrated every year on 3 December with novenas beginning on 24 November.

1. Life Cycle: Tuna are pelagic (open-ocean dwelling) fish that undergo a complex life cycle. 2. Diet: The diet of tuna varies by species, but most feed on other fish and squid. Some tuna, such as the bluefin, also eat crustaceans like crabs and shrimp. Tuna are fast swimmers and powerful predators, able to capture prey in the open ocean.

3. Habitat: Tuna are found in all the world's oceans, from the surface to depths of over 1,000 meters (3,280 feet). They prefer warm waters and can be found near the equator or in tropical regions. Some species migrate seasonally, following food sources or breeding grounds.

4. Threats: Several factors pose a threat to tuna populations. Overfishing is the biggest concern, with many species being fished at unsustainable levels. This has led to declines in population sizes and concerns about the future of some species. Pollution, climate change, and habitat destruction also impact tuna populations, as do accidental catch in fishing operations targeting other species. Some species, such as the Atlantic bluefin, have been classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Efforts are underway to conserve these species through fishery management, research, and conservation measures.

prompt: What are some ways that people can find fulfillment and happiness in their lives?
response:
1. Cultivate a sense of purpose: People who have a clear understanding of their values, goals, and aspirations tend to experience higher levels of fulfillment and happiness. Identify what truly matters to you and focus on pursuing those things.

2. Practice gratitude: Being thankful for the good things in life can help shift your perspective towards positivity and contentment. Make a habit of reflecting on the blessings in your life daily.

3. Build meaningful relationships: Human connections are crucial to our overall well-being. Spend time with loved ones, join social clubs or groups, volunteer, or participate in community events to foster new friendships.

4. Learn new skills: Continuously growing and expanding your knowledge and abilities can lead to feelings of accomplishment and satisfaction. Whether it's taking up a new hobby, learning a language, or mastering a sport, the process of acquiring new skills is rewarding in itself.

5. Prioritize self-care: Taking care of your physical, emotional, and mental health is essential for happiness and fulfillment. Get enough sleep, eat healthy foods, exercise regularly, and practice stress-reducing techniques like meditation or yoga.

6. Embrace challenges: Instead of shying away from difficulties, view them as opportunities for growth and learning. Overcoming obstacles builds resilience, confidence, and a sense of achievement.

7. Find meaning in service: Contributing to others and making a positive impact in the world can bring immense satisfaction and fulfillment. Volunteer your time, resources, or talents to causes that matter to you.

8. Practice forgiveness: Holding onto grudges and resentments can negatively affect your well-being. Learning to forgive others and yourself fosters inner peace and contentment.

9. Live in the present: Avoid dwelling too much on the past or worrying excessively about the future. Focus on enjoying the current moment and savoring life's simple pleasures.

10. Cultivate optimism: Choosing to see the glass as half full rather than half empty can significantly enhance your happiness and fulfillment. Adopting an optimistic mindset helps us appreciate the good in every situation and remain hopeful for the future.

To effectively clean up asphalt (also known as tar or bitumen) from sidewalks and other surfaces, you can follow these steps:

1. Scrape off any large pieces of asphalt using a putty knife or similar tool. Be careful not to damage the surface below.

2. Sweep up any remaining small fragments and debris with a broom or leaf blower.

3. Apply a solvent-based cleaner specifically designed for removing asphalt. Follow the manufacturer's instructions carefully, as some products may require dilution before use.

4. Use a stiff-bristled brush or a power washer (on a low setting) to scrub the affected area thoroughly. Pay special attention to corners, edges, and cracks where asphalt is more likely to accumulate.

5. Rinse the area thoroughly with water to remove all traces of the cleaner and asphalt residue.

6. Allow the surface to dry completely before walking on it or applying any sealants or coatings. This may take several hours, depending on the size of the area and the humidity level.

Some additional tips:

- Wear protective gloves, goggles, and clothing when handling solvents and cleaning solutions.
- Avoid using high-pressure washers near electrical outlets, windows, or other sensitive areas.
- If possible, clean up asphalt spills as soon as they occur to prevent them from hardening and becoming more difficult to remove.
- Consider applying a sealer or coating to the affected area to prevent future asphalt buildup.

By following these steps, you should be able to effectively clean up asphalt from sidewalks and other surfaces without causing any further damage or disruption.

Background: Fear of cancer recurrence or progression (FCR/P) is a common challenge experienced by people living with and beyond cancer and is frequently endorsed as the highest unmet psychosocial need amongst survivors. This has prompted many cancer organizations to develop self-help resources for survivors to better manage these fears through psychoeducation, but little is known about whether they help reduce FCR/P.

Method: We recruited 62 women with ovarian cancer. Women reported on their medical history and demographic characteristics and completed the Fear of Progression Questionnaire-Short Form (FoP-Q-SF). They then read a booklet on FCR specifically created for Ovarian Cancer Australia by two of the authors (ABS and PB). One week after reading the booklet, 50/62 women (81%) completed the FoP-Q-SF and answered questions about their satisfaction with the booklet.

Results: More than half of the women (35/62; 56.5%) scored in the clinical range for FCR/P at baseline. Of the completers, 93% said that they would recommend the booklet to other women. Satisfaction with the booklet was relatively high (75.3/100) and more than two-thirds of women rated it as moderately helpful or better. However, FCR/P did not change significantly over the week following reading the booklet [t(49) = 1.71, p = 0.09]. Some common characteristics of mutts include:

1. Variable size: Mutt pups can range from tiny teacup-sized dogs to large, sturdy breeds. Their adult size will depend on the breeds that make up their heritage.

2. Coat color and texture: Muts can have a wide variety of coat colors and textures due to the mix of genes they inherit from their parents. Some may have short, sleek coats while others may have long, fluffy fur.

A sturdy limb within my tree's embrace,

The world around me, a different place.

My song of life, no longer sung,
The wind that whispered, now willed,
My solace, gone and done.

Beneath the earth, I'll rest my head,

After all, it can activate reward circuits in the brain that also light up in response to drugs like cocaine, and it is possible to build up a tolerance to and dependence on sugar. Studies have shown that sweet or fatty foods can activate pathways in the brain associated with pleasure and reward, kicking off processes that can compete with or override signals that regulate normal hunger and satiety, sometimes causing people to overeat out of pleasure, not hunger. And while salt, sugar, and fat are all tasty on their own, food scientists—and food companies, as noted in a 2013 book aptly titled Salt Sugar Fat: How the Food Giants Hooked Us—have long known they become irresistible when they come together. The hedonic effect may even transcend a candy bar’s ingredients, Pojednic says. “We have these really complex neurologic systems where learning and memory and pleasure all come together,” she explains. “That’s why when you walk into the office and you see that Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup, your mouth literally starts watering.
